# Preface {.unnumbered}

**Draft 0.7.**

*Answers in back* keeps each exercise's answer out of sight until you turn to the appendix, which is what you want while you are still trying to solve it; *answers inline* puts each answer directly below its question, which is what you want when you are reviewing. On this website the answers are always inline but hidden behind a click, so it behaves like the first while reading and the second when you check yourself.
:::

This book was created to accompany students in the course *Statistics and Data Science: a broad perspective*, taught at Utrecht University. I have made heavy use of AI tooling throughout, and I take responsibility for the final text.

As the title suggests, my goal in this book is to cover as much of the landscape as possible. Since that cannot be done in full, I have chosen  **not** to explain any of the analysis techniques, such as GLM, SEM, random forests, neural networks, etc. in much technical depth. There are already plenty of excellent books and other resources out there that do this, which are referenced throughout the text, as well as included in some of the recommendations for further reading below. (And, for students in the MSc program, they will be encountered in your subsequent coursework.) Instead, I have tried to put all these techniques and models into a common perspective, based on a few overarching principles:

 * The bias-variance tradeoff;
 * Explanation and prediction in social and health sciences;
 * The logic of how research questions, design, modeling, and the strength of conclusions all tie in with each other.

The latter may sound somewhat mysterious to you, so here is a summary:

> A research question motivates a design for collecting or organizing data; the design makes a set of assumptions plausible; those assumptions are the model; and the results of fitting the model answer the question, to the extent that the assumptions hold.

The chapters work through this logic. First the logic itself (@sec-rq-to-interpretation). Then, concretely, how to build a statistical model out of a theory stated in words (@sec-theory-to-glm), and what happens when the design cannot answer the question at all (@sec-identification). Then the analysis of variance, often regarded as old-fashioned, is shown to lead to multilevel models and to meta-analysis (@sec-anova). A transitional chapter asks what prediction is for (@sec-explanation-prediction). The last three chapters cross into machine learning: what overfitting is and why the bias-variance tradeoff governs every model (@sec-overfitting), how to evaluate predictions honestly, from cross-validation and the bootstrap to what happens when a well-scored model is put to use (@sec-evaluation), and how all this changes when there is no outcome to predict and the task is to find groups (@sec-unsupervised).

Each chapter contains two kinds of exercises. Inline exercises appear throughout; do them immediately, and click to reveal the answer below each one. The "Test yourself" exercises at the end of each chapter are harder. The practical exercises use R but, everything can be done in Python too. 

The upshot of my choice for this book is that you may sometimes like to consult other texts to study a particular model in more depth. That is intended; my hope is that by following your own interests in this regard, you can keep sight of the big picture and gain a "broad perspective".

Here are a few recommendations for further study.

**Closest to this book.**

- James, G., Witten, D., Hastie, T., & Tibshirani, R. (2021). *An Introduction to Statistical Learning: With Applications in R* (2nd ed.). Springer. Free PDF at [statlearning.com](https://www.statlearning.com/); a Python edition followed in 2023. Covers the machine learning of chapters 6 and 7 at greater length and with more worked examples, at about the same level of difficulty. Read it first if you want more practice rather than more theory.

**Regression, and the models of chapters 2 and 4.**

- Gelman, A., & Hill, J. (2007). *Data Analysis Using Regression and Multilevel/Hierarchical Models*. Cambridge University Press. The standard treatment of the multilevel models this book reaches through the analysis of variance.
- Gelman, A., Hill, J., & Vehtari, A. (2020). *Regression and Other Stories*. Cambridge University Press. The modern successor to Gelman and Hill; free companion material at [avehtari.github.io/ROS-Examples](https://avehtari.github.io/ROS-Examples/).
- Agresti, A. (2018). *An Introduction to Categorical Data Analysis* (3rd ed.). Wiley. The accessible entry for categorical outcomes.
- Agresti, A. (2013). *Categorical Data Analysis* (3rd ed.). Wiley. The comprehensive reference behind it.

**Latent variables and measurement.**

- Beaujean, A. A. (2014). *Latent Variable Modeling Using R: A Step-by-Step Guide*. Routledge. A practical bridge from the equations of chapter 2 to fitted models; the [lavaan website](https://lavaan.ugent.be/) has free tutorials for the software this book uses.
- Saris, W. E., & Stronkhorst, L. H. (1984). *Causal Modelling in Nonexperimental Research: An Introduction to the LISREL Approach*. Sociometric Research Foundation. Still the clearest source on the logic of building and testing such models; a revised version is in preparation and will be linked here when it is finished.

**Design and causal inference, behind chapter 3.**

- Pearl, J., Glymour, M., & Jewell, N. P. (2016). *Causal Inference in Statistics: A Primer*. Wiley. The short introduction to graphs and identification.
- Cunningham, S. (2021). *Causal Inference: The Mixtape*. Yale University Press. Free online at [mixtape.scunning.com](https://mixtape.scunning.com/); works through the designs with data and code.
- Angrist, J. D., & Pischke, J.-S. (2009). *Mostly Harmless Econometrics: An Empiricist's Companion*. Princeton University Press. The econometric view of the same designs.
- Shadish, W. R., Cook, T. D., & Campbell, D. T. (2002). *Experimental and Quasi-Experimental Designs for Generalized Causal Inference*. Houghton Mifflin. The classic on validity and design, and the source of much of chapter 1's vocabulary.
- Hernán, M. A., & Robins, J. M. (2020). *Causal Inference: What If*. Chapman & Hall/CRC. Free at [miguelhernan.org/whatifbook](https://miguelhernan.org/whatifbook). More challenging, and the reference for the potential-outcomes machinery.

**More theory, and the deep end.**

- Hastie, T., Tibshirani, R., & Friedman, J. (2009). *The Elements of Statistical Learning: Data Mining, Inference, and Prediction* (2nd ed.). Springer. The mathematical version of the machine learning chapters, freely available from [the authors' page](https://hastie.su.domains/ElemStatLearn/); it assumes more linear algebra and statistics than this book does.
- Goodfellow, I., Bengio, Y., & Courville, A. (2016). *Deep Learning*. MIT Press. Free to read at [deeplearningbook.org](https://www.deeplearningbook.org/); goes where chapter 6 only gestures.

The source, the data-preparation scripts and the issue tracker live at [github.com/daob/stads-book](https://github.com/daob/stads-book); corrections are welcome.
